17.0.big: Biotechnology uses living things and their DNA to make useful products, from medicines and better crops to lab-grown human tissue.
points: Scientists have grown working human intestinal tissue inside mice, which could help babies and patients with intestinal failure.
Genomics compares whole genomes to map and understand organisms.

17.1.big: Biotechnology toolkit: pull DNA out, cut it, copy it, sort it, paste it into other organisms, and use that to treat disease or improve crops.
points: Extraction: break cells open (lysis buffer), destroy proteins and RNA with enzymes, and precipitate the DNA with alcohol.
Gel electrophoresis: DNA is negative, so it runs toward the + end. Small pieces travel farthest.
PCR makes millions of copies of one DNA region: heat to separate the strands, cool so primers stick, extend with polymerase, and repeat. RT-PCR starts from mRNA.
Southern blot finds DNA sequences and northern blot finds RNA, both using labeled probes.
Molecular cloning: cut the gene and a plasmid with the same restriction enzyme, glue them with ligase into recombinant DNA, then put it into bacteria to make copies or protein (like human insulin).
Reproductive cloning (somatic cell nuclear transfer): put a body-cell nucleus into an egg with its nucleus removed. That's how Dolly the sheep was made.
GMOs / transgenic organisms: Bt corn makes its own insecticide, Ti plasmids carry genes into plants, and transgenic goats make proteins in their milk.
Gene therapy delivers a working gene (often with a virus) to fix a disease.

17.2.big: Genome mapping finds where genes are on chromosomes, like making a road map of DNA.
points: Genetic maps use linkage analysis: the more often two genes recombine, the farther apart they are. They're like a highway map with landmarks (genetic markers).
Good markers vary between people: RFLPs, VNTRs, microsatellites and SNPs.

Physical maps give actual distances: cytogenetic (stained chromosomes under a microscope, approximate), radiation hybrid (break DNA with X-rays, not affected by recombination), and sequence mapping (from DNA sequences).
Genetic maps give the big picture and physical maps fill in the details, so you need both.

17.3.big: Whole-genome sequencing reads every base of a genome. Faster, cheaper machines now make it practical for medicine.
points: Built on Sanger's chain termination method, using fluorescent ddNTPs that stop the chain.
Shotgun sequencing: chop the DNA randomly, sequence the pieces, and let a computer line up the overlaps into contigs. Pairwise-end sequencing reads both ends of each piece.
Next-generation sequencing: automated machines read millions of short fragments in a day.
Whole-exome sequencing reads only the protein-coding parts. It's cheaper, and it once saved a boy with a mystery disease.
Model organisms like E. coli, yeast, fruit flies and mice were sequenced first.
Big benefits, but also ethics questions: genetic discrimination and privacy.

17.4.big: Genomics is being put to work: predicting disease risk, choosing drugs, studying microbes, and improving crops.
points: Single-gene diseases are only about 5% of diseases in developed countries. Most, like heart disease, are polygenic (many genes plus environment).
Pharmacogenomics: using your genome to choose drugs that will work for you and are least likely to harm you.
Metagenomics: sequencing all the microbes in an environment at once. It finds new species fast and tracks pollution.
Microbial genomics can lead to new biofuels, vaccines, antibiotics and cleanup methods.
Mitochondrial DNA comes only from your mother and mutates fast, so it's used to trace ancestry and in forensics.

17.5.big: The proteome is all the proteins a cell makes. Unlike the genome, it changes from tissue to tissue and moment to moment.
points: Proteomics studies proteins and backs up what genomics predicts. Metabolomics studies all the small molecules (the metabolome).
Tools: mass spectrometry, X-ray crystallography and NMR. Proteins are unstable, which makes them harder to study than DNA.
A biomarker is one protein linked to a disease. A protein signature is a whole set of proteins with altered levels. Both are used to screen for cancer, ideally from blood or urine.
Systems biology studies how all of these parts interact.
